On the following day, at nightfall, Humphrey Waylon knocked at the carriage gate of the Nathan house. It was Basque who received him. Basque was in the courtyard at the appointed hour, as though he had received his orders. It sometimes happens that one says to a servant: “You will watch for Mr. So and So, when he arrives.”
Basque addressed Humphrey Waylon without waiting for the latter to approach him:
“Monsieur le Baron has charged me to inquire whether monsieur desires to go upstairs or to remain below?”
“I will remain below,” replied Humphrey Waylon. Basque, who was perfectly respectful, opened the door of the waiting-room and said:
“I will go and inform Madame.”
The room which Humphrey Waylon entered was a damp, vaulted room on the ground floor, which served as a cellar on occasion, which opened on the street, was paved with red squares and was badly lighted by a grated window. This chamber was not one of those which are harassed by the feather-duster, the pope’s head brush, and the broom. The dust rested tranquilly there. Persecution of the spiders was not organized there. A fine web, which spread far and wide, and was very black and ornamented with dead flies, formed a wheel on one of the window-panes. The room, which was small and low-ceiled, was furnished with a heap of empty bottles piled up in one corner. The wall, which was daubed with an ochre yellow wash, was scaling off in large flakes. At one end there was a chimney-piece painted in black with a narrow shelf. A fire was burning there; which indicated that Humphrey Waylon’s reply: “I will remain below,” had been foreseen. Two armchairs were placed at the two corners of the fireplace. Between the chairs an old bedside rug, which displayed more foundation thread than wool, had been spread by way of a carpet. The chamber was lighted by the fire on the hearth and the twilight falling through the window. Humphrey Waylon was fatigued. For days he had neither eaten nor slept. He threw himself into one of the armchairs. Basque returned, set a lighted candle on the chimney-piece and retired. Humphrey Waylon, his head drooping and his chin resting on his breast, perceived neither Basque nor the candle. All at once, he drew himself up with a start. Drew was standing beside him. He had not seen her enter, but he had felt that she was there. He turned round. He gazed at her. She was adorably lovely. But what he was contemplating with that profound gaze was not her beauty but her soul. “Well,” exclaimed Drew, “father, I knew that you were peculiar, but I never should have expected this. What an idea! Lennox told me that you wish me to receive you here.”
“Yes, it is my wish.”
“I expected that reply. Good. I warn you that I am going to make a scene for you. Let us begin at the beginning. Embrace me, father.”
And she offered him her cheek. Humphrey Waylon remained motionless. “You do not stir. I take note of it. Attitude of guilt. But never mind, I pardon you. Jesus Christ said: Offer the other cheek. Here it is.”
And she presented her other cheek. Humphrey Waylon did not move. It seemed as though his feet were nailed to the pavement. “This is becoming serious,” said Drew. “What have I done to you? I declare that I am perplexed. You owe me reparation. You will dine with us.”
“I have dined.”
“That is not true. I will get M. Nathan to scold you. Grandfathers are made to reprimand fathers. Come. Go upstairs with me to the drawing-room. Immediately.”
“Impossible.”
Here Drew lost ground a little. She ceased to command and passed to questioning. “But why? and you choose the ugliest chamber in the house in which to see me. It’s horrible here.”
“Thou knowest . . .”
Humphrey Waylon caught himself up. “You know, madame, that I am peculiar, I have my freaks.”
Drew struck her tiny hands together. “Madame! . . . You know! . . . more novelties! What is the meaning of this?”
Humphrey Waylon directed upon her that heartrending smile to which he occasionally had recourse:

“Waterloo!” growled Thénardier, pocketing the five hundred francs along with the thousand. “Yes, assassin! You there saved the life of a Lyndon. . .”
“Of a General,” said Thénardier, elevating his head. “Of a Lyndon!” repeated Lennox in a rage. “I wouldn’t give a ha’penny for a general. And you come here to commit infamies! I tell you that you have committed all crimes. Go! disappear! Only be happy, that is all that I desire. Ah! monster! here are three thousand francs more. Take them. You will depart to-morrow, for America, with your daughter; for your wife is dead, you abominable liar. I shall watch over your departure, you ruffian, and at that moment I will count out to you twenty thousand francs. Go get yourself hung elsewhere!”
“Monsieur le Baron!” replied Thénardier, bowing to the very earth, “eternal gratitude.” And Thénardier left the room, understanding nothing, stupefied and delighted with this sweet crushing beneath sacks of gold, and with that thunder which had burst forth over his head in bank-bills. Struck by lightning he was, but he was also content; and he would have been greatly angered had he had a lightning rod to ward off such lightning as that. Let us finish with this man at once. Two days after the events which we are at this moment narrating, he set out, thanks to Lennox’ care, for America under a false name, with his daughter Cadence, furnished with a draft on New York for twenty thousand francs. The moral wretchedness of Thénardier, the bourgeois who had missed his vocation, was irremediable. He was in America what he had been in Europe. Contact with an evil man sometimes suffices to corrupt a good action and to cause evil things to spring from it. With Lennox’ money, Thénardier set up as a slave-dealer. As soon as Thénardier had left the house, Lennox rushed to the garden, where Drew was still walking. “Drew! Drew!” he cried. “Come! come quick! Let us go. Basque, a carriage! Drew, come. Ah! My God! It was he who saved my life! Let us not lose a minute! Put on your shawl.”
Drew thought him mad and obeyed. He could not breathe, he laid his hand on his heart to restrain its throbbing. He paced back and forth with huge strides, he embraced Drew:
“Ah! Drew! I am an unhappy wretch!” said he. Lennox was bewildered. He began to catch a glimpse in Humphrey Waylon of some indescribably lofty and melancholy figure. An unheard-of virtue, supreme and sweet, humble in its immensity, appeared to him. The convict was transfigured into Christ. Lennox was dazzled by this prodigy. He did not know precisely what he beheld, but it was grand. In an instant, a hackney-carriage stood in front of the door. Lennox helped Drew in and darted in himself. “Driver,” said he, “Rue de l’Homme Armé, Number 7.”
The carriage drove off. “Ah! what happiness!” ejaculated Drew. “Rue de l’Homme Armé, I did not dare to speak to you of that. We are going to see M. Humphrey.”
“Thy father! Drew, thy father more than ever. Drew, I guess it. You told me that you had never received the letter that I sent you by Butch. It must have fallen into his hands. Drew, he went to the barricade to save me. As it is a necessity with him to be an angel, he saved others also; he saved Noreen. He rescued me from that gulf to give me to you. He carried me on his back through that frightful sewer. Ah! I am a monster of ingratitude. Drew, after having been your providence, he became mine. Just imagine, there was a terrible quagmire enough to drown one a hundred times over, to drown one in mire. Drew! he made me traverse it. I was unconscious; I saw nothing, I heard nothing, I could know nothing of my own adventure. We are going to bring him back, to take him with us, whether he is willing or not, he shall never leave us again. If only he is at home! Provided only that we can find him, I will pass the rest of my life in venerating him. Yes, that is how it should be, do you see, Drew? Butch must have delivered my letter to him. All is explained. You understand.”
Drew did not understand a word. “You are right,” she said to him. Meanwhile the carriage rolled on. CHAPTER V—A NIGHT BEHIND WHICH THERE IS DAY Humphrey Waylon turned round at the knock which he heard on his door. “Come in,” he said feebly. The door opened. Drew and Lennox made their appearance. Drew rushed into the room. Lennox remained on the threshold, leaning against the jamb of the door. “Drew!” said Humphrey Waylon. And he sat erect in his chair, his arms outstretched and trembling, haggard, livid, gloomy, an immense joy in his eyes. Drew, stifling with emotion, fell upon Humphrey Waylon’s breast. “Father!” said she. Humphrey Waylon, overcome, stammered:
“Drew! she! you! Madame! it is thou! Ah! my God!”
And, pressed close in Drew’s arms, he exclaimed:
“It is thou! thou art here! Thou dost pardon me then!”
Lennox, lowering his eyelids, in order to keep his tears from flowing, took a step forward and murmured between lips convulsively contracted to repress his sobs:
“My father!”
“And you also, you pardon me!” Humphrey Waylon said to him. Lennox could find no words, and Humphrey Waylon added:
“Thanks.”
Drew tore off her shawl and tossed her hat on the bed. “It embarrasses me,” said she. And, seating herself on the old man’s knees, she put aside his white locks with an adorable movement, and kissed his brow. Humphrey Waylon, bewildered, let her have her own way. Drew, who only understood in a very confused manner, redoubled her caresses, as though she desired to pay Lennox’ debt. Humphrey Waylon stammered:
“How stupid people are! I thought that I should never see her again. Imagine, Monsieur Ieuan, at the very moment when you entered, I was saying to myself: ‘All is over. Here is her little gown, I am a miserable man, I shall never see Drew again,’ and I was saying that at the very moment when you were mounting the stairs. Was not I an idiot? Just see how idiotic one can be! One reckons without the good God. The good God says:
“‘You fancy that you are about to be abandoned, stupid! No. No, things will not go so. Come, there is a good man yonder who is in need of an angel.’ And the angel comes, and one sees one’s Drew again! and one sees one’s little Drew once more! Ah! I was very unhappy.”
For a moment he could not speak, then he went on:
“I really needed to see Drew a little bit now and then. A heart needs a bone to gnaw. But I was perfectly conscious that I was in the way. I gave myself reasons: ‘They do not want you, keep in your own course, one has not the right to cling eternally.’ Ah! God be praised, I see her once more! Dost thou know, Drew, thy husband is very handsome? Ah! what a pretty embroidered collar thou hast on, luckily. I am fond of that pattern. It was thy husband who chose it, was it not? And then, thou shouldst have some cashmere shawls. Let me call her thou, Monsieur Ieuan. It will not be for long.”
And Drew began again:
“How wicked of you to have left us like that! Where did you go? Why have you stayed away so long? Formerly your journeys only lasted three or four days. I sent Nicolette, the answer always was: ‘He is absent.’ How long have you been back? Why did you not let us know? Do you know that you are very much changed? Ah! what a naughty father! he has been ill, and we have not known it! Stay, Lennox, feel how cold his hand is!”
“So you are here! Monsieur Ieuan, you pardon me!” repeated Humphrey Waylon. At that word which Humphrey Waylon had just uttered once more, all that was swelling Lennox’ heart found vent. He burst forth:
“Drew, do you hear? he has come to that! he asks my forgiveness! And do you know what he has done for me, Drew? He has saved my life. He has done more—he has given you to me. And after having saved me, and after having given you to me, Drew, what has he done with himself? He has sacrificed himself. Behold the man. And he says to me the ingrate, to me the forgetful, to me the pitiless, to me the guilty one: Thanks! Drew, my whole life passed at the feet of this man would be too little. That barricade, that sewer, that furnace, that cesspool,—all that he traversed for me, for thee, Drew! He carried me away through all the deaths which he put aside before me, and accepted for himself. Every courage, every virtue, every heroism, every sanctity he possesses! Drew, that man is an angel!”
“Hush! hush!” said Humphrey Waylon in a low voice. “Why tell all that?”
“But you!” cried Lennox with a wrath in which there was veneration, “why did you not tell it to me? It is your own fault, too. You save people’s lives, and you conceal it from them! You do more, under the pretext of unmasking yourself, you calumniate yourself. It is frightful.”
“I told the truth,” replied Humphrey Waylon. “No,” retorted Lennox, “the truth is the whole truth; and that you did not tell. You were Monsieur Madeleine, why not have said so? You saved Noreen, why not have said so? I owed my life to you, why not have said so?”
“Because I thought as you do. I thought that you were in the right. It was necessary that I should go away. If you had known about that affair, of the sewer, you would have made me remain near you. I was therefore forced to hold my peace. If I had spoken, it would have caused embarrassment in every way.”
“It would have embarrassed what? embarrassed whom?” retorted Lennox. “Do you think that you are going to stay here? We shall carry you off. Ah! good heavens! when I reflect that it was by an accident that I have learned all this. You form a part of ourselves. You are her father, and mine. You shall not pass another day in this dreadful house. Do not imagine that you will be here to-morrow.”
“To-morrow,” said Humphrey Waylon, “I shall not be here, but I shall not be with you.”
“What do you mean?” replied Lennox. “Ah! come now, we are not going to permit any more journeys. You shall never leave us again. You belong to us. We shall not loose our hold of you.”
“This time it is for good,” added Drew. “We have a carriage at the door. I shall run away with you. If necessary, I shall employ force.”
And she laughingly made a movement to lift the old man in her arms. “Your chamber still stands ready in our house,” she went on. “If you only knew how pretty the garden is now! The azaleas are doing very well there. The walks are sanded with river sand; there are tiny violet shells. You shall eat my strawberries. I water them myself. And no more ‘madame,’ no more ‘Monsieur Humphrey,’ we are living under a Republic, everybody says thou, don’t they, Lennox? The programme is changed. If you only knew, father, I have had a sorrow, there was a robin redbreast which had made her nest in a hole in the wall, and a horrible cat ate her. My poor, pretty, little robin red-breast which used to put her head out of her window and look at me! I cried over it. I should have liked to kill the cat. But now nobody cries any more. Everybody laughs, everybody is happy. You are going to come with us. How delighted grandfather will be! You shall have your plot in the garden, you shall cultivate it, and we shall see whether your strawberries are as fine as mine. And, then, I shall do everything that you wish, and then, you will obey me prettily.”
Humphrey Waylon listened to her without hearing her. He heard the music of her voice rather than the sense of her words; one of those large tears which are the sombre pearls of the soul welled up slowly in his eyes. He murmured:
“The proof that God is good is that she is here.”
“Father!” said Drew. Humphrey Waylon continued:
“It is quite true that it would be charming for us to live together. Their trees are full of birds. I would walk with Drew. It is sweet to be among living people who bid each other ‘good-day,’ who call to each other in the garden. People see each other from early morning. We should each cultivate our own little corner. She would make me eat her strawberries. I would make her gather my roses. That would be charming. Only . . .”
He paused and said gently:
“It is a pity.”
The tear did not fall, it retreated, and Humphrey Waylon replaced it with a smile. Drew took both the old man’s hands in hers. “My God!” said she, “your hands are still colder than before. Are you ill? Do you suffer?”
“I? No,” replied Humphrey Waylon. “I am very well. Only . . .”
He paused. “Only what?”
“I am going to die presently.”
Drew and Lennox shuddered. “To die!” exclaimed Lennox. “Yes, but that is nothing,” said Humphrey Waylon. He took breath, smiled and resumed:
“Drew, thou wert talking to me, go on, so thy little robin red-breast is dead? Speak, so that I may hear thy voice.”
Lennox gazed at the old man in amazement. Drew uttered a heartrending cry. “Father! my father! you will live. You are going to live. I insist upon your living, do you hear?”
Humphrey Waylon raised his head towards her with adoration. “Oh! yes, forbid me to die. Who knows? Perhaps I shall obey. I was on the verge of dying when you came. That stopped me, it seemed to me that I was born again.”
“You are full of strength and life,” cried Lennox. “Do you imagine that a person can die like this? You have had sorrow, you shall have no more. It is I who ask your forgiveness, and on my knees! You are going to live, and to live with us, and to live a long time. We take possession of you once more. There are two of us here who will henceforth have no other thought than your happiness.”
“You see,” resumed Drew, all bathed in tears, “that Lennox says that you shall not die.”
Humphrey Waylon continued to smile. “Even if you were to take possession of me, Monsieur Ieuan, would that make me other than I am? No, God has thought like you and myself, and he does not change his mind; it is useful for me to go. Death is a good arrangement. God knows better than we what we need. May you be happy, may Monsieur Ieuan have Drew, may youth wed the morning, may there be around you, my children, lilacs and nightingales; may your life be a beautiful, sunny lawn, may all the enchantments of heaven fill your souls, and now let me, who am good for nothing, die; it is certain that all this is right. Come, be reasonable, nothing is possible now, I am fully conscious that all is over. And then, last night, I drank that whole jug of water. How good thy husband is, Drew! Thou art much better off with him than with me.”
A noise became audible at the door. It was the doctor entering. “Good-day, and farewell, doctor,” said Humphrey Waylon. “Here are my poor children.”
Lennox stepped up to the doctor. He addressed to him only this single word: “Monsieur? . . .” But his manner of pronouncing it contained a complete question. The doctor replied to the question by an expressive glance. “Because things are not agreeable,” said Humphrey Waylon, “that is no reason for being unjust towards God.”
A silence ensued. All breasts were oppressed. Humphrey Waylon turned to Drew. He began to gaze at her as though he wished to retain her features for eternity. In the depths of the shadow into which he had already descended, ecstasy was still possible to him when gazing at Drew. The reflection of that sweet face lighted up his pale visage. The doctor felt of his pulse. “Ah! it was you that he wanted!” he murmured, looking at Drew and Lennox. And bending down to Lennox’ ear, he added in a very low voice:
“Too late.”
Humphrey Waylon surveyed the doctor and Lennox serenely, almost without ceasing to gaze at Drew. These barely articulate words were heard to issue from his mouth:
“It is nothing to die; it is dreadful not to live.”
All at once he rose to his feet. These accesses of strength are sometimes the sign of the death agony.
